clinicalPearls: Most common in the short tubular bones of the hand (phalanges, metacarpals), where it is frequently discovered incidentally or after a pathological fracture through the thinned cortex.
Classic radiographic appearance is a well-defined lucent medullary lesion with a lobulated margin and chondroid matrix mineralisation described as rings, arcs, stippling or a popcorn pattern.
Endosteal scalloping of less than roughly two-thirds of the cortical thickness favours a benign enchondroma; deep scalloping, cortical breach or periosteal reaction raise concern for chondrosarcoma.
In long bones (proximal femur, humerus) it is genuinely difficult to distinguish from low-grade (grade 1) chondrosarcoma, and clinical correlation with pain and lesion size is essential.
MRI shows a lobulated lesion of high T2 signal with peripheral and septal ring-and-arc enhancement, reflecting the avascular hyaline cartilage lobules.

Multiple lesions define an enchondromatosis: Ollier disease (multiple enchondromas) and Maffucci syndrome (enchondromas with soft-tissue and visceral haemangiomas), both carrying a substantially increased risk of malignant transformation.
Somatic mosaic IDH1 and IDH2 mutations underlie many sporadic enchondromas and the enchondromatoses.
Asymptomatic hand lesions are simply observed; symptomatic or fractured lesions are treated with curettage with or without bone grafting.
reference.pathophysiology: Enchondroma is a benign intramedullary neoplasm of mature hyaline cartilage that is thought to arise from displaced or retained rests of physeal (growth-plate) cartilage that fail to undergo normal endochondral ossification and instead persist and slowly enlarge within the medullary cavity. The lesion is composed of lobules of hypocellular hyaline cartilage separated by fibrovascular or bony septa, with mineralisation occurring by enchondral ossification and dystrophic calcification. Somatic mosaic gain-of-function mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 and IDH2, producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, are implicated in sporadic lesions and, when acquired early in development, in the multifocal enchondromatoses (Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome), which explains their metaphyseal distribution and elevated risk of progression to chondrosarcoma.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs in two orthogonal planes as the initial and often definitive study
MRI to characterise cartilage lobules, marrow involvement and any soft-tissue component
CT to define matrix mineralisation, endosteal scalloping and cortical integrity
Bone scintigraphy, noting that active enchondromas may show uptake and cannot alone exclude malignancy
Image-guided or open biopsy reserved for lesions with worrying features, accepting the risk of sampling error in heterogeneous cartilage tumours
Assessment for enchondromatosis and family history when multiple lesions are present
redFlags: New or increasing rest or night pain not attributable to fracture
Growth or change of a cartilage lesion in a skeletally mature adult
Cortical destruction, periosteal reaction or an associated soft-tissue mass
Deep endosteal scalloping exceeding two-thirds of cortical thickness or a lesion larger than about 5 to 6 cm in a long bone
Multiple lesions with clinical features of Ollier or Maffucci syndrome
reference.prognosis: Solitary enchondromas have an excellent prognosis with low recurrence after curettage and a very low rate of malignant transformation. The risk of secondary chondrosarcoma is appreciably higher in the enchondromatoses, warranting long-term surveillance.
pitfalls: Overcalling a benign enchondroma as chondrosarcoma, or the reverse, particularly for long-bone lesions where imaging overlap is marked
Relying on biopsy alone, since sampling error in heterogeneous cartilage tumours can under-grade a malignancy
Mistaking a mineralised bone infarct for an enchondroma or vice versa
Failing to arrange surveillance for long-bone lesions and for patients with enchondromatosis

Resnick, Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Observation with serial radiographic surveillance for asymptomatic solitary lesions, given the excellent prognosis and very low malignant potential
Curettage and bone grafting for symptomatic lesions, those at risk of pathological fracture, or lesions in the short tubular bones of the hand
Fixation and treatment of pathological fractures, often allowing the fracture to heal before curettage
Careful distinction from low-grade chondrosarcoma using pain, lesion size, degree of endosteal scalloping and cortical integrity, with biopsy reserved for worrying features
Wide surgical resection where malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is suspected
Long-term surveillance and assessment for enchondromatosis such as Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome when multiple lesions are present, given their higher malignant-transformation risk
Referral to a specialist bone-tumour and orthopaedic-oncology multidisciplinary team for indeterminate or aggressive lesions
